title.value: Wasserstein Dependency Measure for Representation Learning
title.justification: The paper's title is mentioned multiple times throughout the document, especially in the header and conclusion sections.
title.quote: Wasserstein Dependency Measure for Representation Learning

analysis.description: The paper addresses the limitations of mutual information maximization in unsupervised representation learning by introducing the Wasserstein dependency measure. The authors provide an empirical analysis demonstrating that mutual information-based approaches often fail to learn complete representations, especially in tasks with high mutual information like video understanding or reinforcement learning. They propose using the Wasserstein distance as a substitute, claiming this approach yields more complete representations by overcoming the fundamental limitations of KL divergence used in mutual information estimators. Theoretical motivations and practical approximations through Lipschitz constraint techniques from GAN literature are discussed and evaluated across several tasks.

type.justification: The paper provides empirical demonstrations and experiments comparing the model's performance across various tasks and datasets.
type.quote: In this work, we empirically demonstrate that mutual information-based representation learning approaches do fail to learn complete representations on a number of designed and real-world tasks. To mitigate these problems, we introduce the Wasserstein dependency measure.

name.justification: The paper focuses on learning effective representations in the unsupervised learning setting, particularly overcoming challenges associated with mutual information estimators.
name.quote: representation learning in the unsupervised setting, without hand-specified labels, becomes significantly more challenging: although much more data is available for learning, this data lacks the clear learning signal that would be provided by human-specified semantic labels. Nevertheless, unsupervised representation learning has made significant progress recently

name.justification: The paper mentions and evaluates self-supervised learning techniques as part of its scope and comparisons.
name.quote: Self-supervised learning techniques have demonstrated state-of-the-art performance in speech and image understanding (van den Oord et al., 2018; Hjelm et al., 2018), reinforcement learning (Jaderberg et al., 2016; Dwibedi et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2018), imitation learning (Sermanet et al., 2017; Aytar et al., 2018), and natural language processing (Devlin et al., 2018; Radford et al.)

name.justification: The paper uses GAN literature techniques for Lipschitz constraint methods to develop practical approximations to the proposed solution.
name.quote: constructed using Lipschitz constraint techniques from the GAN literature, achieves substantially improved results on tasks where incomplete representations are a major challenge.

name.justification: The paper introduces Wasserstein Predictive Coding as an approximation to the theoretical Wasserstein dependency measure and evaluates its effectiveness in empirical tasks.
name.quote: We propose a new objective, which is a lower bound on both contrastive predictive coding and the dual Wasserstein dependency measure, by keeping both the Lipschitz class of functions and the log exp, which we call Wasserstein predictive coding (WPC).

is_contributed.justification: WPC is introduced as a new method within the paper to improve representation learning outcomes where previous methods failed.
is_contributed.quote: We propose a new objective, which is a lower bound on both contrastive predictive coding and the dual Wasserstein dependency measure.

is_executed.justification: Experiments involving WPC are reported, demonstrating its application in practice.
is_executed.quote: Figures 4(a), and 5(a) show the performance of CPC and WPC as we vary the dataset size.

is_compared.justification: WPC's performance is compared against Contrastive Predictive Coding (CPC) throughout the experiments section.
is_compared.quote: Figures 4(a), and 5(a) show the performance of CPC and WPC as we vary the dataset size.
